data.title: OUTKICK POSTS STRONG GROWTH IN Q3 2026
data.description:
OUTKICK POSTS STRONG GROWTH IN Q3 2026

OUTKICK POSTS STRONG GROWTH IN Q3 2026

PR Newswire

NEW YORK, Oct. 16, 2026

 The Platform Also Saw Year Over Year Growth in September

NEW YORK, Oct. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- National multimedia sports platform OutKick completes Q3 2026 with significant growth across all categories. The platform finished with 12.2 million average monthly desktop and mobile unique visitors, up 40% versus the prior quarter and up 149% versus the prior year quarter, 190 million total multiplatform views, up 56% versus the prior quarter and up 187% versus the prior year quarter, and 201 million total multiplatform minutes, up 29% versus the prior quarter and up 196% versus the prior year quarter, according to Comscore.*

Additionally, OutKick in September 2026 delivered 12.8 million total desktop and mobile unique visitors, up 188% versus the prior year, 64 million multiplatform views, up 192% versus the prior year, and 62 million total multiplatform minutes, up 213% versus the prior year, according to Comscore.

In commenting on the digital performance, OutKick's senior vice president and managing editor Gary Schreier said, "OutKick's quarterly numbers reflect the platform's continued growth and influence across sports and culture. Throughout the quarter, OutKick broke sport industry news involving ESPN, drove the conversation around Sophie Cunningham, and delivered on-the-ground coverage for college football and the NFL. This speaks to OutKick's commitment to providing authentic and in-depth stories shaping the sports landscape." 

On Facebook, X (formerly Twitter), and Instagram in Q3 2026, OutKick saw over 3 million social actions, up 58% versus the prior quarter and over 27.3 million total video views, up 22% versus the prior quarter on Facebook, X and YouTube, according to ComscoreSocial.*** 

In September, OutKick also announced the signing of Matt Calkins, the former Seattle Times sports columnist, who joined the platform to cover sports and culture. 

*Source: Comscore Media Metrix® Multi-Platform, September 2026, Desktop and Mobile, US.

**Source: Comscore Media Metrix® Multi-Platform, September 2026, Total Digital Population, US

***Source: Comscore Social, Metrics & Trends, Facebook, Instagram, X, YouTube, September 2026, Report Date: 10/15/2026. Custom-Defined List including Outkick.

About OutKick
OutKick is one of the fastest growing national multimedia platforms that produces and distributes engaging content at the intersection of sports, sports culture, pop culture, and news. OutKick's industry recognized stable of reporters, hosts and contributors are accessible on FoxNews.com/OutKick as well as across video livestreams, social media, podcasts, and radio, reaching tens of millions of fans each month. Owned by Fox Corporation, OutKick was originally founded by Clay Travis. For more information, please visit FoxNews.com/OutKick.

###

OutKick Press Contact:
Brian Karpas
212-301-9966
brian.karpas@outkick.com

 "Being recognized as a Best Workplace in Technology reflects that curiosity and the people who bring it to life every day."

The Best Workplaces in Technology award is based on analysis of survey responses from nearly 144,000 employees from Great Place To Work Certified™ companies in the tech industry.

Being recognized as a Best Workplace in Technology reflects that curiosity and the people who bring it to life every day."

The Best Workplaces in Technology list is highly competitive. Survey responses reflect a comprehensive picture of the workplace experience. Honorees were selected based on their ability to offer positive outcomes for employees regardless of job role, work status or other demographic identifier.

"Congratulations to the Fortune Best Workplaces in Technology," says Michael C. Bush, CEO of Great Place To Work. "People are at the heart of work in every industry and technology is no exception. These companies show how delivering for your people drives financial performance and turns fear of the future into the confidence to win."

Read about the various recognitions Invisors has received this year from Great Place to Work across the US and UK at https://www.invisors.com/news.

As a certified Workday Services Partner, Invisors helps customers utilize their organizational data to make better-informed business decisions through the deployment of Workday. We believe the most important measure of our team's success is our client's ability to achieve their big-picture vision. From initial deployments to ongoing projects, we are focused on elevating perspectives + transforming results. Learn more by visiting invisors.com.

About the Fortune Best Workplaces in Technology List

Great Place To Work selected the 2026 Best Workplaces in Technology by analyzing confidential survey responses from more than 1.3 million employees in the U.S., representing the experiences of over 7.3 million employees in 2025 and 2026. Of those responses, nearly 144,000 came from employees at Great Place To Work Certified companies in the technology industry and this ranking is based on that feedback. Companies with 10 to 999 employees competed in the small and medium category. Companies with 1,000 or more employees were considered for the large category.

As the global authority on workplace culture, Great Place To Work, a UKG company, brings 30 years of groundbreaking research and data to help every place become a great place to work for all. Its proprietary platform and Great Place To Work Model help companies evaluate the experience of every employee, with exemplary workplaces becoming Great Place To Work Certified and receiving recognition on a coveted Best Workplaces list.

data.title: I'm 64 with two sons, but only one works in the family firm. Should I leave him 70% of the business?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'I have some reservations about the long-term stability of my younger son's marriage'

"My retirement is fully funded, and I have sufficient assets to cover long-term care should the need arise." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I am 64 years old and financially secure. My retirement is fully funded, and I have sufficient assets to cover long-term care should the need arise. I am widowed and have no intention of remarrying. I own a business that I estimate would be worth $500,000-600,000 if sold today. I have two sons, ages 36 and 32.

My family and business: My older son (Son #1) has worked alongside me for 11 years and has played a significant role in building the business. My younger son (Son #2) is married, lives about an hour away, and works in the computer industry. He has a degree in computer engineering, and his wife has a master's degree in engineering and is also well employed.

My current estate plan: My will currently provides for Son #1 to inherit 60% of the business, with his share increasing by 2% for each additional year he works in the business. He would then buy out his brother's remaining interest. I believe this is fair, given Son #1's years of service and contributions. My other assets, totaling $6 million, are divided equally.

My current thinking: As I approach retirement, I would like to transfer ownership of the business to Son #1. I recognize that transferring it to him would affect the inheritance ultimately received by Son #2. One option I am considering is gifting 70% of the business to Son #1 at its current fair market value, with an agreed-upon price and terms for him to buy out Son #2's 30%. Naturally, I would work with my attorney and CPA to structure any arrangement appropriately.

My main concern: The one complication is that I have some reservations about the long-term stability of my younger son's marriage. They have been married for four years, have no children, and do not intend to have any. I sincerely hope their marriage lasts, but I cannot say I have complete confidence that it will. I would prefer that those funds be protected to the extent legally possible, rather than potentially becoming part of a marital property dispute.

With that in mind, I have wondered whether the buyout could be structured so that payments would not begin for another five or even 10 years.

My Questions:

-- Does gifting 70% of the business to Son #1, while establishing an agreement for him to purchase the remaining 30% from Son #2, seems like a reasonable approach?

-- Could the buyout be structured with deferred payments or other provisions to help protect the funds Son #2 eventually receives in the event of a divorce?

I understand that the details will need to be worked out with my attorney and CPA, but I would appreciate hearing your perspective and ideas before moving forward.

The Father

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: 'I feel like a loser': My stock portfolio is swinging wildly. Is it finally time to worry?

Equal inheritances, which come with a step-up in basis for tax purposes, are not necessarily equal inheritances.

Dear Father,

It doesn't need to be so complicated.

Fair is not always equal: Your business, while clearly of significance to your life's work, probably because it was something you created from scratch and you would like to see it continue, makes up just 8% of your estate. With that in mind, why not give Son #1 this $500,000 to $600,000 business, when the time comes, and deduct it from the rest of his inheritance so both sons receive equal shares of your estate? That seems like the most straightforward plan.

Of course, equal inheritances, which come with a step-up in basis for tax purposes, are not necessarily equal inheritances. Son #1 has spent 11 years working alongside you and helping to build a business, and you may understandably and rightfully feel that his contributions - how do I put this delicately? - warrant some additional consideration. You may wish to reflect that 70/30 split in your estate plan. That does not seem unreasonable to me.

Marital vs. separate property

Inheritance is separate property, but it may become marital property if it is commingled. Even without a prenuptial or, indeed, a postnuptial agreement, you can set up a trust for your sons. A properly drafted discretionary trust with spendthrift provisions may offer greater protection against a 'y's creditors and marital claims. The trust can specify whether they receive the money as an income rather than a lump sum, for instance.

This may be preferable to a lump sum that could accidentally (or not) be commingled as marital property. Things get more complicated if you give a lump sum to your children during your lifetime. You would have to fill out IRS Form 709 federal gift-tax return, although filing a return does not necessarily mean you owe gift tax. For 2026, the federal lifetime estate and gift tax exemption is $15 million per person, and the annual gift-tax exclusion is $19,000 per recipient.

You want to avoid a Cain and Abel situation. As one member of the Moneyist Facebook Group noted: "As a CPA, I'm glad you're thinking about this proactively. Unfortunately, I often have to deal with the aftermath when these issues haven't been thought through in advance. I think leaving the entire business to Son #1 is a smart move for several reasons. DO NOT PUT PEOPLE INTO A PARTNERSHIP THEY DON'T WANT!" (The all-caps format is his.)

Avoiding family conflict

Your final calculation should account for the business's fair market value. "The goal should be to avoid putting the kids in a business partnership that could lead to conflict, especially if divorce is a possibility," he wrote. "Otherwise, you could inadvertently put Son #1 in business with his ex-sister-in-law. The key is to plan ahead, be intentional about how the assets are distributed, and avoid creating future conflicts in an effort to make everything appear equal."

You also asked whether payments could be deferred for five or even 10 years. An installment sale or promissory note could certainly make that happen, but I'd be wary of stretching payments out that far just to protect Son #2 in case of divorce. A deferred payment obligation doesn't automatically shield the proceeds from marital claims, and the note itself may be treated as an asset in a divorce.

Beneficiaries vs. wills

A lifetime or beneficiary-controlled trust living trust is effective for wealthy individuals with spouses. For families with complex estates, consolidating accounts and assets under one trustee can help everything run more smoothly. Beneficiary designations can become problematic if they contradict what a person has written in their will (a beneficiary designation would take precedence over a will), so make sure your messaging is consistent.

Smith Debnam, a law firm with offices in North and South Carolina, has an opinion on such a predicament. "While you may love your son-in-law or daughter-in-law, you may not necessarily want to pass your assets to them," it says. "Many people have reservations about this scenario. After all, your son-in-law or daughter-in-law could remarry and the assets you worked a lifetime to accumulate could end up benefiting their new spouse."

"A testamentary trust is a trust created in a will. When you die, if the trust is 'triggered,' the trust springs into being," the law firm adds. "A revocable living trust, also simply referred to as a revocable trust, is a separate estate planning document you create and fund during your lifetime. It operates in much the same way as a testamentary trust after your death, but can also be used to control assets during your lifetime."

Consider separate trusts for each of your sons.

data.title: Retiring abroad? Don't cut these financial ties to the U.S.
data.description:
By Edd and Cynthia Staton

Think carefully about your Social Security, Medicare, credit cards and bank accounts before picking your new home overseas.

Before you choose a home overseas, think about the financial logistics of your move.

People considering retirement abroad devote countless hours of research to finding the "perfect" place.

They compare weather, cost of living, healthcare, crime statistics, visa requirements and whether to rent or buy.

Meanwhile, some of the more mundane questions get ignored.

How do I deal with Medicare? Where should Social Security be deposited? Do I keep my American bank account? What happens to my U.S. credit score? Can I get a credit card in my new country?

And here's one rarely considered thought: What am I going to do about my mailing address and phone number?

We certainly didn't have all those bases covered when we moved to Cuenca, Ecuador, 16 years ago. Over time, we have learned there are really two parts to moving abroad.

Narrowing down the right location is the exciting part that most people focus on.

Then there are the financial and logistical matters that are often pushed to the side. Failing to consider this humdrum second category can create unnecessary confusion and aggravation.

Here are some key things to consider before you pack the suitcases.

Do I have to give up my U.S. citizenship?

A common misconception is that moving abroad requires relinquishing your U.S. citizenship and passport. In reality, unless you relocate to one of the few countries that offer fast-track "citizenship by investment" programs, this choice isn't even a possibility.

An application for legal residency must happen first. This is often a two-step process of temporary and then permanent status that takes several years. Afterward, each country has its own rules for the length of time residents must wait before becoming eligible for citizenship.

Even if that option is chosen, most countries allow dual citizenship. That means that relinquishing U.S. citizenship is a choice, not a requirement.

Even for entry, many foreign countries require your passport to show at least six months of remaining validity. Unless you have recently renewed your U.S. passport, doing so before relocation abroad gives you 10 years until the next expiration date.

Why do I need an address of record?

Keeping an address of record in the U.S. is a good idea, even if you are moving to another country.

If you plan to maintain a banking relationship in the United States, federal law requires you to provide a physical address to prove your identity. A post office box or mail-receiving agency does not qualify.

Credit-card companies need an address to send replacement cards. Banks have the same requirement for debit cards.

Medicare Advantage and prescription-drug plans are tied to specific geographic locations. To enroll in these programs, you must have an address in the area the plan serves.

What if you've sold a residence or were renting? In this case, a trusted family member or friend can be enormously helpful for receiving the occasional piece of mail, replacement credit card or other documents that still must be sent the old-fashioned way.

Simply having a U.S. mailing address doesn't automatically demonstrate you legally reside in that state. Residency can affect taxes, voting, driver's licenses, insurance and other matters, and the rules in every state are different.

How do I keep a U.S. phone number?

Retaining a U.S. phone number means staying in touch with friends and loved ones is so much easier. But international plans with major carriers can cost $100+ per month.

Fortunately, there are affordable and even free options available. Our phone numbers are through Tello, a mobile virtual-network operator that rents tower space from T-Mobile. Rates start as low as $5 per month. In most countries, a Wi-Fi connection is required.

Many people around the world stay connected through WhatsApp. It's totally free and easy to set up. When connected to Wi-Fi, you can make unlimited voice or video calls, send texts, plus share photos, videos and large files to anyone with an active WhatsApp account.

What should I do about Medicare?

Original Medicare does not provide coverage beyond U.S. borders, and some Medicare Advantage plans offer only worldwide benefits for emergencies. If you are a senior moving to another country, should you keep it or opt out?

In our 16+ years living in Cuenca, we have seen innumerable instances of people arriving with the intent of never living in the United States again. But a personal health emergency arises. Grandchildren tug at the heartstrings. Or being an expat doesn't turn out as expected.

And they find themselves on a plane heading home.

Initially refusing Medicare and applying later, or canceling and reapplying, triggers a late-enrollment penalty. For every year without Part B coverage, you permanently add an extra 10% to your current monthly premium.

Example: You opt out and re-enroll 10 years later. You've added an extra 100% (10% x 10 years) to your payment as long as you continue coverage.

Our strong advice is to enroll in Medicare when you become eligible or, if you are already receiving benefits, continue your coverage when you move abroad. You never know what the future holds.

Should I close my U.S. bank account?

We don't recommend rushing to close your U.S. bank account because you may find it extremely useful when living abroad.

You can pay existing installment and revolving debt, receive Social Security payments (more on that next), handle tax payments and refunds and transfer money between countries.

This isn't an either/or decision. A local bank account in your new country can be helpful. Our Ecuador savings account simplifies daily life since we have it set up to automatically pay ongoing bills for utilities, cellphone service and internet.

Where should Social Security be deposited?

The choice is up to you. The Social Security Administration will deposit benefits into a U.S. bank even if you live overseas. The SSA also offers international direct deposit into financial institutions in many countries.

If you are concerned about constantly transferring money from the United States and paying foreign transaction and/or ATM fees, international direct deposit could be more convenient.

Look for banks that allow you to receive Social Security payments abroad without service charges or foreign transaction fees.

What about credit cards?

When you reside outside the United States, your credit history doesn't follow you. That means you can have decades of spotless credit in America and still be a ghost to a financial institution in another country.

For this reason, obtaining a credit card abroad can be difficult when you first arrive. The same is true for mortgages. Home purchases often require all cash, and in countries that do offer mortgages to foreign buyers, be prepared to put up to 50% down and pay higher rates.

To keep your credit score active, retain and continue to use at least one U.S. credit card. We recommend using one that doesn't charge foreign transaction fees.

Don't forget Uncle Sam

Leaving the United States doesn't mean waving goodbye to the U.S. tax system. American citizens living abroad generally remain subject to U.S. tax-filing requirements on worldwide income.

Opening a local bank account can also inadvertently create additional reporting obligations. If the combined value of your foreign financial accounts exceeds $10,000 at any point during the year, you may have to file a Foreign Bank Account Report (FBAR).

Depending on the value of your total foreign assets, other reporting requirements can apply as well. Consulting a tax professional experienced with Americans living overseas about your personal circumstances is advised.

Your homework assignment

Going on vacation temporarily gets you away from your regular life. When you move abroad, you are relocating that life.

Along with fantasizing about exotic locations and charming apartments, we encourage you to spend some time on the boring yet important daily life stuff.

Renew your passport. Organize your phone number and mailing address. Evaluate Medicare options. Decide where Social Security payments will go. Protect your U.S. credit history. Understand your tax obligations.

Then go back to looking at those beachfront condos with beautiful views and trendy historic lofts, all the while dreaming about your future adventures.

Take it from these two longtime expats - it's all worth it.

-Edd and Cynthia Staton

data.title: 'It's a wait-and-see situation': I'm 63 and diagnosed with lymphoma. Should I take my Social Security next year?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'My plan is to continue working as long as I'm able to do so and invest my Social Security benefits while I'm still earning a paycheck'

"It may remain stable, or it could progress, so for now, it's a wait-and-see situation." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I'd like your thoughts, please. I'll be turning 64 next January and have been thinking about starting my Social Security benefits then. I was diagnosed with lymphoma. It may remain stable, or it could progress, so for now, it's a wait-and-see situation. Am I overlooking anything or missing something important in considering this strategy? I'd appreciate any thoughts or advice.

My plan is to continue working as long as I can and invest my Social Security benefits while I'm still earning a paycheck. I understand there's a limit to how much you can earn before reaching full retirement age without affecting your benefits, and I believe I'd be earning around that limit.

When I'm 64

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: 'I feel like a loser': My stock portfolio is swinging wildly. Is it finally time to worry?

Given the uncertainty surrounding your diagnosis, it's smart to regularly evaluate your financial security.

Dear (Almost) 64,

I'm sorry you're dealing with such a serious diagnosis on top of what is already a tricky decision. Your plans are realistic and optimistic, which is a good combination. If you are the lower-earning spouse, I see no problem with taking your Social Security in 2027. There is one caveat: if you claim at 64, applying for disability benefits later may not be an option if your lymphoma progresses. Before you decide, ask Social Security or a financial adviser how claiming early would affect that.

Here's the trade-off: If you live well into your 80s, delaying benefits will result in higher lifetime monthly payments. Because a survivor's benefit is based on the deceased spouse's claiming age, a delay by the higher earner also means a larger benefit for the surviving spouse. If your health deteriorates, claiming earlier means you will enjoy your benefits now. Given the uncertainty surrounding your diagnosis, it's smart to regularly evaluate your financial security.

The earnings test is a big issue. Before full retirement age, Social Security withholds $1 in benefits for every $2 you earn above the annual limit ($24,480 in 2026). You say that you are currently earning "around that limit," and you also write that you make a good living. If you earn well above it, most or all of your benefits could be withheld, leaving no checks to invest. Social Security recalculates your benefits at retirement age so that money withheld is not lost.

You'll also have to account for any taxes on your investments. The Internal Revenue Service calculates tax due on your Social Security based on your "combined income," which consists of your adjusted gross income, tax-exempt interest, and half of your annual Social Security benefits. So up to 50% or as much as 85% of your Social Security benefits may be subject to federal income tax. Stacking benefits on top of a good salary makes that more likely.

If you live well into your 80s, delaying benefits will result in higher lifetime monthly payments.

When you reach full retirement age (67 for you, given your age), the Social Security earnings test no longer applies, so working won't reduce your monthly benefit. And while your Social Security benefits may be taxable on your federal return, some states do not tax Social Security benefits. So, given that you are still working and earning a good income, I understand your idea of investing your checks.

For married couples filing jointly, Social Security benefits typically aren't taxable at the federal level if your combined annual income is $32,000 or less. Between $32,000 and $44,000, up to 50% of benefits may be taxable; above $44,000, up to 85% may be taxable. These thresholds apply to combined income. See the IRS's Social Security benefits guidance and use Box 5 of your SSA-1099 when preparing your tax return.

If you keep working and collect Social Security, being taxed on your Social Security can sting, given that you are already paying 6.2% of your wages toward Social Security, in addition to the 6.2% that your employer contributes. That's because it goes toward a collective fund so Americans who can no longer work and/or wish to retire have a source of income. A tax adviser would be best able to run through all the scenarios.

Predicting the math

Your Social Security benefit at 64 would be reduced by 20% compared with your FRA. So let's assume that your benefit at age 64 is $2,000 a month; your FRA benefit at 67 would be close to $2,500 per month. Delaying from 67 to 70 increases the retirement benefit by 24%, before cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs). If your investments had a hypothetical 10% annual return before inflation, investing your checks might look attractive.

Let's take two scenarios: one with a 10% return and another with a more modest 7% return. If you invested your $2,000-a-month Social Security at 64, you could accumulate a lot in contributions, growing to roughly $80,000 at 7% or $83,500 at 10%, before taxes and fees. The exact total depends on the timing of your deposits, compounding, taxes and fees. The market rarely runs smoothly, and some years see a negative return, so nothing is guaranteed.

Obviously, waiting to collect your Social Security until 67 or later provides no accumulated investment, but your benefit would be higher by about $500 a month for life. Without investing, that extra $500 takes about 12 years to make up the $72,000 head start, so the break-even is roughly 79. If you claim at 64 and invest the benefits, the break-even point versus waiting until age 67 depends on your benefit, returns, capital-gains taxes, dividends, and how long you live.

Without investing, it would take about 12 years to make up the $72,000 head start.

A few reminders about the rules of survivor benefits: A surviving spouse who has reached FRA can generally receive up to 100% of their deceased spouse's benefit. You or your husband would not ordinarily receive both full retirement benefits added together. Instead, the survivor generally receives their own benefit or an eligible survivor benefit, with the applicable rules determining the amount payable. This is important if you are the higher earner.

Your diagnosis raises two other points. First, claiming reduced retirement benefits early could leave you worse off. If you can no longer work, you may qualify for Social Security Disability Insurance, which pays your full retirement age benefit without reductions that come from claiming early. (Some lymphomas are on Social Security's Compassionate Allowances list.) Second, Medicare begins at 65, with the Part B premium deducted from your Social Security.

Even taking your diagnosis into account, I wouldn't count out a long life just yet. The 10-year survival rates for lymphoma vary based on whether it is Hodgkin lymphoma or non-Hodgkin lymphoma, as well as the stage, your age, and the subtype. Survival statistics are very general and only give a glimpse into lymphoma mortality rates. Your oncology team is best placed to discuss your situation, assuming you want to factor that into your decision-making.

So what should you do? The fact that you're asking the question suggests that you're inclined to take your benefits earlier and keep working. Compare your actual Social Security estimates at 64, 67, and 70, and check how the earnings test will impact you for the years you plan to claim. If you are the higher-earning spouse, you may wish to wait. If your husband is the higher-earning spouse, he may wish to wait before claiming to maximize survivor benefits.

It's also not an apples-to-apples comparison. A delayed benefit provides you with a guaranteed income for life that is also adjusted for inflation. Investment returns are, as we know, uncertain.

Two Summit Care Facilities Named to Newsweek's 2027 List of America's Best Nursing Homes

Two Summit Care Facilities Named to Newsweek's 2027 List of America's Best Nursing Homes

PR Newswire

LUTZ, Fla., Oct. 16, 2026

LUTZ, Fla., Oct. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Newsweek's list of America's Best Nursing Homes for 2027 ranked Tampa Lakes Health and Rehabilitation, operated by Summit Care in Lutz, Florida, #40 in the category of facilities with more than 150 beds. Including just facilities with 50-99 beds, Surrey Place Healthcare & Rehabilitation, operated by Summit Care in Bradenton, Florida, achieved a third-place ranking. In addition to its award-winning journalism, Newsweek publishes rankings and recognition lists that highlight organizations and institutions across a range of industries, including health care.

"We're very proud that our facilities were recognized by Newsweek among the best nursing homes in the country," said Isabelle Jean-OBrien, V.P. of Marketing and Business Development, Summit Care. "This honor reflects our team's unwavering commitment to delivering high-quality care and creating environments where residents feel safe, supported, and valued. Our dedicated staff makes a difference in the lives of our residents every day, and we remain focused on strengthening the communities we serve and enhancing the quality of life for each of our residents."

Each year, Newsweek collaborates with global data research firm Statista to rigorously evaluate and rank nursing homes across the United States. America's Best Nursing Homes 2027 highlights 1,325 of the nation's top nursing homes out of 14,693 analyzed. The evaluation is based on performance data, peer recommendations, accreditations and satisfaction and uses Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) data.

Summit Care Management
Summit Care Management is a healthcare consulting and management company specializing in skilled nursing and assisted living care. Summit partners with healthcare facilities to identify challenges, strengthen operations, and implement strategies that drive quality outcomes. They provide expert consultants who identify challenges and develop tailored plans across clinical services, reimbursement, business operations, billing, IT, personnel management, marketing, and therapy services, with a strong focus on quality outcomes. In addition, they deliver essential administrative support including accounts payable, cash flow management, payroll processing, technical support, and financial reporting. Their mission is to assist each facility in providing quality-focused care while improving operational efficiency.

For more information about Summit Care Management and its dedication to quality skilled nursing and rehabilitation care, visit www.summitcare.com.

data.title: HealthEdge Investment Partners Announces Todd Cooper As Operating Partner
data.description:
HealthEdge Investment Partners Announces Todd Cooper As Operating Partner

HealthEdge Investment Partners Announces Todd Cooper As Operating Partner

PR Newswire

TAMPA, Fla., Oct. 16, 2026

TAMPA, Fla., Oct. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- HealthEdge Investment Partners, LLC ("HealthEdge") is pleased to announce that Todd Cooper has joined its team of Operating Partners. Mr. Cooper will work alongside HealthEdge's investment team and portfolio company management teams to support growth and operational improvement and assist in evaluating new investment opportunities.

Mr. Cooper currently serves as Lead Director at three HealthEdge portfolio companies: Alatus Solutions, Custom Protect Ear, and Veridian Healthcare. His appointment builds on these existing relationships and expands his involvement across the firm's investment and portfolio management efforts.

Mr. Cooper brings extensive executive leadership experience across healthcare services, medical devices and distribution, and business services. He also has extensive experience providing strategic direction and partnering with management teams to drive meaningful value creation, developed over several years as a senior partner in management consulting. Prior roles include leading Secure, Presbia and NVISION, as well as serving as Vice President and General Manager of Henry Schein Medical. His background includes managing both public and private companies across medical transportation, ophthalmology and medical and surgical products.  His board experience spans private, public, and private equity backed companies, giving him a broad perspective across ownership structures and business environments. 

HealthEdge Managing Partner Phil Dingle said, "Todd brings extensive healthcare operating experience and a practical understanding of the opportunities and challenges facing growing businesses. Through his leadership at Alatus Solutions, Custom Protect Ear, and Veridian Healthcare, we have seen firsthand the value he brings to our management teams. We are pleased to welcome him as an Operating Partner and look forward to his expanded involvement across HealthEdge."

Mr. Cooper added, "I have enjoyed working with the HealthEdge team and its portfolio company leaders, and I am excited to expand that relationship as an Operating Partner. HealthEdge's collaborative approach and emphasis on operating experience align closely with how I work with businesses. I look forward to helping our management teams pursue their next stage of growth."

ABOUT HEALTHEDGE INVESTMENT PARTNERS

HealthEdge Investment Partners is an operating-oriented private equity firm founded in 2005 that focuses exclusively on the healthcare industry. HealthEdge partners with founders and management teams of lower middle-market healthcare businesses, providing capital and operating expertise to support growth and long-term value creation. For more information, please visit www.healthedgepartners.com

data.title: Vortex Promotes Dan Watson to EVP, Vortex International; Appoints James Sargeant as SVP, Managing Director, UK & Ireland
data.description:
Vortex Promotes Dan Watson to EVP, Vortex International; Appoints James Sargeant as SVP, Managing Director, UK & Ireland

Vortex Promotes Dan Watson to EVP, Vortex International; Appoints James Sargeant as SVP, Managing Director, UK & Ireland

PR Newswire

HOUSTON, Oct. 16, 2026

Leadership appointments reinforce Vortex's long-term international strategy and continued investment in UK and European markets.

HOUSTON, Oct. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Vortex Companies (Vortex), a global leader in trenchless infrastructure rehabilitation solutions, is pleased to announce the promotion of Dan Watson to Executive Vice President, Vortex International, and the appointment of James Sargeant as Senior Vice President and Managing Director of UK & Ireland services. These leadership appointments reflect the company's growing presence across the UK and Europe and its commitment to building a stronger, more integrated international business.

"Our vision for Vortex has always extended beyond the markets we serve today," said Mike Vellano, CEO of Vortex Companies. "Dan has been instrumental in establishing our international presence, building relationships and identifying opportunities that position us for long-term success. His promotion reflects our confidence in his leadership and our commitment to putting the right people in place to scale the business. "With Dan leading our international strategy and experienced executives like James joining the team, we have the leadership in place to drive international growth, scale our services, and expand our capabilities to meet growing market demand."

Watson will oversee the strategic development and integration of Vortex's international operations, with a focus on strengthening the company's position across the UK, Europe and emerging global markets. Supporting this strategy, Sargeant will lead Vortex's UK and Ireland Services operations, with responsibility for operational performance, business development and advancing the company's installation and rehabilitation services.

"James brings exactly the type of experience and leadership we need as we enter the next phase of our international development," said Watson. "He understands the complexities of the UK infrastructure market and has a proven ability to build teams, strengthen customer relationships and deliver operational results."

James will play a key role in advancing the services business and ensuring it has the operational capacity to support customer needs. "I'm excited to join Vortex at such an important stage in its international growth," said Sargeant. "The company has built an impressive portfolio of rehabilitation solutions, supported by highly experienced teams. My priority will be to build on that foundation."

"Together, Watson and Sargeant will be instrumental in executing Vortex's long-term international strategy, combining strategic vision with operational leadership to strengthen and scale our existing, fully integrated business across the UK and Europe. Their appointments reinforce Vortex's position as the global leader in trenchless infrastructure rehabilitation and our commitment to strengthening our international operations and delivering exceptional value to our customers."

About Vortex Companies
With more than 65 locations worldwide, Vortex Companies is a global provider of trenchless water and sewer infrastructure solutions, delivering advanced technologies and turnkey services for the rehabilitation, replacement and protection of critical infrastructure. Vortex specialises in pipe, manhole and structure rehabilitation and manufactures CIPP liners, geopolymer and hybrid mortars, polymeric coatings, resins and grouts. Its technology portfolio also includes UV curing systems, sewer robotics and high-speed drain-cleaning equipment. For more information, visit www.vortexcompanies.com.

data.title: The stock market has already crashed: Why a Wall Street veteran says Nike is the ultimate turnaround trade.
data.description:
By Barbara Kollmeyer

Larry McDonald says consumers are too stressed to handle many more Fed rate hikes

Nike is one beaten-down stock that Wall Street veteran Larry McDonald sees on a comeback path over the next two years.

Investors worried about a broader stock market collapse, fear not. A meltdown has already happened with lots of stocks having tumbled in value, according to Wall Street veteran Larry McDonald.

Even with the S&P 500 SPX recently reaching a fresh record high, the market has "crashed internally," McDonald, author of The Bear Traps Report, told the Julia La Roche show in an interview that was published on Thursday. "If you look at the amount of Hall of Fame brands, Harley-Davidson, down 30%, 40%, Lennar, 45%, just really great American brands," getting crushed, he said.

Need to Know: Nearly 40% of the S&P 500 is in a bear market. Here are 10 of those stocks that analysts say can gain up to 81%.

He blamed the disconnect between those record highs and individual stocks being sold on a passive investment system that is getting "more broken." As retirement funds and inflows from exchange-traded funds push more money at big tech names, index funds like State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust SPY stay healthy on the surface. That gap is widening as institutional and hedge funds, also referred to as the smart money, take long positions in the index and short - betting against an asset - lots of individual names.

Also contributing is quarter-end and year-end tax-loss selling - unloading the worst-performing stocks to lower capital-gains burdens - from mutual funds and individual investors. Stocks already under pressure sell off even further, while other companies' stocks are sold just for those tax-loss strategies.

McDonald, former vice president of distressed debt and convertible securities at Lehman Brothers, is also worried about the convertible-bond market - bonds that can be converted into shares of common stock by the issuer - specifically with neocloud companies. CoreWeave (CRWV), for example, spooked stock markets earlier this week. Its high-yield bonds tumbled amid worries over the pace of borrowing and whether AI investments will ultimately pay off.

McDonald said CoreWeave is a "serial convertible issuer." Past examples of companies repeatedly coming to that market for funding included Tyco and Enron. Therefore, "it's a real warning sign because it's the last saloon."

"The last two times we saw this was in 1999 and 2021, and in both cases, this was incredibly foreshadowing for an event coming at us," he said. The dot-com crash followed in 2000, while 2022 proved a losing year for stocks, especially tech names partly due to rising U.S. interest rates.

As for the Federal Reserve, he said he is taking the contrarian view that three interest rate cuts are far more likely than three more hikes. He sees consumer-facing companies - McDonald's (MCD), Home Depot (HD), Netflix (NFLX), Nike (NKE) and Lululemon (LULU) - "under massive stress," with shares down by double-digit percentages this year. That's as consumers battle rising energy and other costs.

He said he expects possibly one more Fed interest-rate increase before its members "tip their hand to a softer path." For that reason, he said now is an opportune moment to invest in gold and silver, pointing to monetary easing triggering a bull market for commodities. Precious metals tend to rise when interest rates are falling. Gold prices (GC00) are down 3% this year so far, while silver (SI00), off 18%, is looking like "one of the best-looking trades" for the next 12 months, he said.

"I like silver because you've got the data-center spending. Solar is like absolutely crazy ripping globally. Like the amount of solar capacity coming online in the United States and China. That's all bullish for silver," he said, adding that U.S. households are underowned when it comes to precious metals.

McDonald is also interested in one of those beaten-down consumer stocks, Nike, down around 50% from its 52-week high. He said many portfolio managers would prefer to own Nvidia headed into 2027 rather than the athletic apparel company that's struggling to engineer a turnaround. He likes Nike for its free cash flow and dividend, which offers something of "downside protection."

Analysts polled by FactSet estimate Nike will generate $1.36 in free cash flow per share over the next 12 months. The stock's Thursday close of $37.14 makes for a forward FCF yield of 3.65%. Nike's current annual dividend is $1.64 a share, which means the stock's dividend yield is 4.42%. That exceeds the forward free cash flow yield and the trailing free cash flow yield of 3.82%.

He said he's watching for one big event that could work in the company's favor in the distant future: "By the Summer Olympics in 2028, if [Nike] is up 100%, 150%, 200% from here, I wouldn't be surprised."

-Barbara Kollmeyer
